# Rice and Maize Disease Research — English Consolidation

This English consolidation preserves the structured disease/source records used by the application. It replaces the original Korean narrative as the working-language document. The original narrative is preserved separately. Collected regulatory, occurrence and licensing claims are research notes, not verified legal or diagnostic advice.

    "Lesion size is 1–3 cm long in IRRI and 0.5–1 cm wide × 1–3 cm long in LSU; NCPMS gives no figure ('size not uniform').",
    "Lesion color: NCPMS dark green with surrounding light brown; IRRI grayish-white center with brown margin; LSU grayish-white or light green center with brown to reddish-brown border; UAEX tan to light-brown center with dark green or brown border.",
    "Timing: IRRI tillering to milk stage, UAEX tillering to booting, LSU infection starting late tillering to internode elongation; NCPMS gives calendar dates such as sclerotium formation in late July to early August.",
    "Humidity thresholds differ: NCPMS 96% or above, UAEX above 95%, IRRI 85–100%. Temperatures are effectively the same: NCPMS 22–35 °C (optimum 30–32 °C) and UAEX 73–95 °F.",
    "The AG1-IA designation appears only in UAEX. The Kim 1994 abstract only says AG-1 IA was isolated from 7 crops, so whether rice isolates were IA is Unconfirmed at the abstract level.",
    "On spores, IRRI and LSU say 'no airborne spores', while UAEX says sexual spores form but are rare in the field."
  ],

    "Severity with late infection: Nongsaro says 'plants usually look like healthy plants', while Lucid says 'chlorosis and mottling are mild, with delayed heading and grain filling', so the range differs.",

    "Tillering conflicts: Wang 2022 says 'normal', Nongsaro and Lucid say 'reduced' (that this may reflect infection timing is an inference in the notes).",
    "Stripe color: Nongsaro 'broad yellow' (yellow-green in resistant cultivars, yellowish-white with late infection), Lucid 'chlorotic to yellowish-white', Wang 'faded green'.",
    "Mortality figures by leaf stage are more specific in Chung 1974 (100% at 3rd–7th leaf, about 50% at 9th, about 20% at 11th) than in Nongsaro; both sources agree on 50% at the 9th leaf stage.",
    "Sap transmission: the ICTV *Tenuivirus* chapter states that mechanical transmission by sap is possible, but Nongsaro says there is no seed, contact or soil transmission. The experimental conditions behind the ICTV statement are Unconfirmed.",
    "Nongsaro D00004257 'rice stripe' is a page for proso millet and must not be confused with the rice page (D00000740)."

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "NCPMS gives fungal growth at 8–37 °C, optimum 25–28 °C, and conidium production at 12–34 °C, without identifying the original experiments. Frequent rain, cool summers including cold injury, humid weather around heading, and excessive nitrogen favor outbreaks. IRRI lists low soil moisture, frequent prolonged showers, cool daytime temperatures, and dew associated with large day–night temperature differences. Silicate application can reduce disease in silicon-deficient soil. Infection thresholds for leaf-wetness duration and relative humidity were not verified. In NCPMS, water-soaked oval lesions that look like they have been blanched grow dark green and the surrounding area turns light brown, and sclerotium is usually written as a 1-2 mm brown circle** ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description and pathogen characteristics).",

        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* A 1-3 cm grey-green oval lesion starting from the leaf sheath near the water surface or ground, with a grey-white center and brown border, and a 1-2 mm brown sclerotium ([IRRI RKB sheath blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/sheath-blight); [NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), pathogen characteristics). However, since it overlaps with other *Rhizoctonia* type sclerotium diseases, it is treated as 'suspicious'.\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Close-up photo of sclerotium, nitrogen fertilization amount, dense planting, and variety ([NCPMS sheath blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000813&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment).\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* The pathogen spreads through mycelium and does not produce airborne spores (IRRI). Rice Doctor attributed the source of sclerotium levels to Chien et al. Write 1969 ([Rice Doctor Sheath blight](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Sheath_blight.htm)).   {
    "no": 3,
    "crop": "rice",
    "user_name": "Brown spot",
    "official_kr_name": "Brown spot",
    "scientific_name": "*Bipolaris oryzae*",
    "kr_occurrence": "Yes (LPDK 1928)",
    "kr_quarantine": "regulated non-quarantine pest (rice seeds)",
    "commercial_image": "Yes (Bugwood alert, Commons CC BY)",
    "section_title": "Brown spot — *Bipolaris oryzae*",
    "fields": {
      "f1_names": {
        "label": "Official names, scientific names, and synonyms",
        "text": "NCPMS lists it as **brown spot** (胡麻葉枯病), and the English name has a typo as \"Heliminthosporium blight, Helminthosporium leaf\". The pathogen is *Cochliobolus miyabeanus* (Ito & Kuribayashi) Drechsler ex Dastur, asexual morph and is listed as *Helminthosporium oryzae*, *Drechslera oryzae*, and *Bipolaris oryzae* ([NCPMS brown spot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y), basic information/pathogen information). LPDK carries the current name *Bipolaris oryzae* (Breda de Haan) Shoemaker, synonym *C. miyabeanus*, English name Helminthosporium blight/leaf spot, Brown spot·Ear blight, and the second national name 'Ear blight' ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), brown spot line). The EPPO preferred name is *B. oryzae*(COCHMI), *Ophiobolus miyabeanus* is added to the synonym, and the English name is brown spot of rice, etc. ([EPPO COCHMI](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHMI), Overview).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y",
          "https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do",
          "https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHMI"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Infects coleoptiles, leaves, leaf sheaths, panicle branches, glumes, and spikelets. Disease occurs at all stages, with infection from maximum tillering to grain filling particularly important (IRRI). NCPMS reports a rapid increase after panicle initiation and greater susceptibility of lower leaves; panicle infection affecting yield occurs up to 25 days after heading. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y)",
        "source_urls": [
          "http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot",
          "https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Small, round, dark-brown to purplish leaf spots enlarge into circular or oval lesions with light-brown to gray centers and reddish-brown margins. Lesions are 5–14 mm in susceptible varieties and pinhead-sized in resistant varieties. Dark-brown to black oval spots occur on glumes and panicle branches; grains develop pecky rice (IRRI). NCPMS describes a yellow toxic halo around the initial dark-brown necrotic area, later concentric rings, and dark-brown streaks on panicle stalks. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y)",
        "source_urls": [
          "http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot",
          "https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "In some varieties, it can be mistaken for rice blast ([IRRI RKB brown spot](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot), last paragraph). It is closely related to abiotic factors: It is common in soils with water stress, nutrient deficiency, and accumulation of toxic substances ([IRRI RKB brown spot](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/brown-spot), Why and where it occurs), and is also common in Korea in old rice fields, peat soils, sandy soils, and shallow hard soils ([NCPMS brown spot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000750&totalSearchYn=Y), occurrence environment). Zinc deficiency is described as similar to iron deficiency/iron toxicity, producing \"dusty brown spots\" in the upper leaves and brown blotches/streaks in the lower leaves, but this page does not directly compare brown spots (indirect evidence) ([Rice Doctor Zinc deficiency](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Zinc_deficiency.htm)).",

      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Causes seedling wilt (kresek) and leaf yellowing and drying. Infection at booting affects grain quality and the proportion of broken rice more than yield (IRRI). In Korea it usually appears around heading, but in regularly affected fields it can occur early in the main field and occasionally in nurseries. Sudden wilting and death can occur from 20–30 days after transplanting through peak tillering. Symptoms mainly affect leaf blades and sheaths, and occasionally grains (NCPMS). [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y)",
        "source_urls": [
          "http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight",
          "https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Water-soaked to yellowish-orange stripes appear at the tip, edge, and wound of the leaf, and the **edge is wavy** as it progresses toward the base of the leaf. On young lesions, milky bacterial ooze forms early in the morning, and when it dries, it turns into yellow beads. Old lesions become yellow to grayish white and black dots appear due to saprophytic microorganisms ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight), How to identify). NCPMS states that infiltrative lesions on the edge 5 to 6 cm below the tip of the leaf blade spread up and down to yellow/orange yellow and fade to white to grayish white after 2 to 3 days ([NCPMS bacterial blight](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y), symptom description).",
        "source_urls": [
          "http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight",
          "https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },

Details of the diagnostic differences are discussed in the differentiation field; photograph-based identification alone does not establish the pathovar. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do)",
        "source_urls": [

        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f5_differentiation": {
        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Yellow-orange to yellow-white lesions with wavy borders starting from the leaf tips and edges, milky ooze drops on young lesions in the early morning, and dry yellow beads ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight)). Contrast with the straight edges of Xoc ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms))\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Squeeze the bottom of the kresek seedling to check for yellow ooze, making sure it is not easily pulled out; Cut a young lesion, place it in clear water, and after a few minutes, see if a cloudy liquid flows from the cut surface ([IRRI RKB bacterial blight](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight), How to identify).       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "IRRI and EPPO list 25–34 °C and RH above 70%; strong winds and prolonged heavy rain disperse bacterial ooze, and excessive nitrogen increases severity. EPPO cites Mew et al. 1993 and identifies floodwater and irrigation as major routes. NCPMS reports high occurrence at July mean temperatures of 22–24 °C, major outbreaks with July rainfall at least 200 mm and winds at least 15 m/s, and disease incidence of 8.8% after 12-hour flooding versus 72.7% after 48-hour flooding. Rainfall from late July to late August is important. Host weeds include *Leersia* grasses; bacteriophage density can provide a warning 10–15 days in advance. The original experiments are not identified. The original report recommends prioritizing Korean values in Korean risk models, with IRRI/EPPO ranges alongside them. [Source 1](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-blight) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet) [Source 3](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000744&totalSearchYn=Y)",

        "text": "Korea: The first literature on LPDK is Mu Nae-kyo, Joseon Dynasty Prefectural Government 5:62 (**1930**) and Lee Gyeong-hwi et al. 1965 ([LPDK](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/english/plntDissInfoMain.do), bacterial blight line). The EPPO datasheet, citing a Korean paper, shows that the domestic occurrence area increased more than 10 times between 2002 and 2005, reaching approximately 27,000 ha (Noh et al. 2007), who wrote that the 2003 outbreak caused large losses with the emergence of a new race **K3a** (Jeung et al. 2006; Original paper not read, re-cited) ([EPPO XANTOR datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTOR/datasheet), Impact). United States: **PPQ select agent**(7 CFR 331.3(b)(6) \"Xanthomonas oryzae\", species-specific pv. *oryzae* included), listed as APHIS Pests of Concern ([US-331](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-331.3); [US-PoC](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/laws-regs/animal-plant-diseases-pests-concern)). Japan: not listed(verified)([JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). Australia: unverified. It is a disease** of *avenae* (Hoo-seop Jeong et al. 1980), and EPPO calls this *Acidovorax* disease “bacterial brown stripe of rice” ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do); [EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Detection paragraph)). EPPO preferred name is *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (Fang et al.) Swings et al. (XANTTO) and the synonym is *X. campestris* pv. *oryzicola*, *X. oryzicola*, *X. translucens* f. sp. *oryzicola*, English name is bacterial leaf streak (BLS) ([EPPO XANTTO](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO), Overview). It was first observed in the Philippines in 1918, but was long mistaken for bacterial blight, and was named *X. oryzicola* in China in 1957, and reclassified as pathovar in 1990 ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Notes on taxonomy).",

        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Primarily affects leaf blades; infected florets become brown or black, and infected seeds show glume browning and endosperm necrosis (EPPO). Effects are important from maximum tillering to panicle initiation, while mature rice recovers more readily (IRRI). Both pathovars have been isolated from the seed coat, but the cited EPPO account reports seed transmission for Xoc only. Xoc can survive for up to 5 months in seed stored at 15–30 °C. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak)",

        "text": "Narrow, dark green water-soaked stripes between leaf veins with a yellow border turn yellow-orange to brown and merge, forming small amber-colored bacterial ooze droplets, which dry out to brown to gray at the end ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms). The lesion is **translucent** when held up to light ([IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak), How to identify). It is often accompanied by moth larvae and rice leaf beetle stains ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Symptoms).",

        "text": "Advanced Xoc leaf streak and Xoo bacterial blight may be difficult to distinguish and may occur on the same leaf. Xoc lesions have straight edges; bacterial-blight lesions have wavy edges. Xoc enters through stomata or wounds and colonizes intercellular spaces in the mesophyll; Xoo enters through hydathodes and colonizes vascular tissue (EPPO). Biochemical, pathogenicity, or serological testing may be needed (IRRI). Narrow brown spot, associated in LPDK with *Cercospora oryzae*, is not translucent and does not produce bacterial ooze. A source comparing abiotic disorders was not verified. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak) [Source 3](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do)",

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "Post-infection temperature is the main determining factor, with progression occurring at 26-32 ℃ and suppression below 22 ℃ (as cited in Devadath 1984). Secondary infections do not occur without sustained rainfall, and only very wet conditions cause damage, and large amounts of nitrogen encourage outbreaks. In water, it survives up to 90 days at 15-20 ℃ and up to 60 days at 25-45 ℃ ([EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Biology paragraphs 5-7). Yield loss is 8-17% in the rainy season, 1-3% in the dry season (IRRI), 5-30% in central India, 10-20% in southern China (up to 40%), and up to 60% in Uganda ([IRRI RKB BLS](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bacterial-leaf-streak), Why is it important; [EPPO XANTTO datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/XANTTO/datasheet), Economic impact).",

        "text": "In the nursery, affected seedlings may grow to at least 1.5 times normal height, then become stunted and die within 1–2 weeks; heavily infected seedlings can die without elongation. IRRI describes slender yellow-green plants, reduced tillering, white powdery fungal growth at the stem base, and roots on above-ground nodes; infected plants can also be stunted or appear normal. Of 15 Korean field isolates of *F. fujikuroi*, 9 caused stunting and 6 caused typical elongating bakanae symptoms; stunting isolates produced no gibberellin or 10–15 times less (Niehaus et al. 2017). [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5675463/)",

If it is determined based solely on outgrowth, the actual latent infection rate can be more than 10 times higher ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752), symptom description).         "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Height difference within the seedbed (more than 1.5 times), light green/yellow-green leaf color, 1st and 2nd true leaves angle 45° or more, 2nd and 3rd true leaves not appearing, white mycelium/spores at the base of the stem, aerial rooting of above-ground nodes, browning of nodes ([NCPMS bakanae disease](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752); [IRRI RKB Bakanae](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae)).)       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "NCPMS reports optimum disease development at a nursery temperature of 35 °C after sowing, disease at about 25 °C, and no symptoms at 20 °C. Fungal growth is optimal at 27–30 °C and sporulation at 24–32 °C; spores disperse at night or in light rain. The aerobic pathogen spreads more readily in upland seedbeds and protected nurseries than flooded seedbeds, and dense sowing increases disease. Secondary infection through main-field soil was not reported in that account. Infected seed is the main source, and contaminated soaking water also spreads the pathogen (IRRI). Quantitative evidence for nitrogen effects was not verified. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000752) [Source 2](http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/training/fact-sheets/pest-management/diseases/item/bakanae)",

LPDK lists *B. glumae* and ***B. plantarii*** together under \"bacterial grain rot / bacterial sheath rot\" (DSNM_NO 1418), and ***B. gladioli* is listed separately** under \"stem blight\" (Sheath rot) ([LPDK search](https://genebank.rda.go.kr/plntDissInfoMain.do), host rice bacteria result table). EPPO (PSDMGM)'s English name is bacterial grain rot, colored rice, ear blight, seedling blight of rice ([EPPO PSDMGM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PSDMGM)).) It is called \"bacterial grain rot\" in Asia and \"bacterial panicle blight\" in the United States and Central and South America. The rice pathogen was transferred to the genus *Burkholderia* in 1994 ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Introduction).       "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "It is mainly rice grain, and there are symptoms in the leaf sheath as well. Infected seeds are unable to germinate and rot, and the seedlings die after browning of the leaf sheath ([NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), symptom description). It overwinters in seeds, spreads to healthy seeds during soaking, and lurks in leaf sheaths before invading rice grains at the heading stage (same page, occurrence environment). The heading and flowering periods are the most vulnerable ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Symptoms). A 2015 Rural Development Administration report stated that \"symptoms appear only on rice grains,\" which is different from NCPMS (\"symptoms even on leaf sheaths\") ([Rural Development Administration press release 2015-07-29](https://korea.kr/news/pressReleaseView.do?newsId=156066598)).",

        "text": "Grains discolor from the base, becoming yellowish white as discoloration spreads. The Arkansas description notes white to light-gray discoloration of the lower third of the glume, separated by a reddish-brown boundary; the panicle axis initially remains green, and dark-brown lesions may occur on the flag-leaf sheath. [Source 1](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742) [Source 2](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf)",

It can be confused with pest damage such as wind damage, water stress (partial infertility), and striped rice stem borer ([FSA7580](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf), Disease Symptoms last paragraph·Fig. 8–9).       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "Domestic: Large outbreaks occur during high temperatures and humidity during the planting and flowering periods. Easily occur when pathogenic bacteria are over 10² CFU/mL and temperatures are over 20 ℃. There is no difference in resistance between domestic varieties ([NCPMS bacterial grain rot](https://ncpms.rda.go.kr/npms/SicknsInfoDtlR.np?sicknsListNo=D00000742), occurrence environment); ** High temperatures over 30 ℃ before and after planting, or frequent rain around 30 mm** ([Rural Development Administration press release) 2015-07-29](https://korea.kr/news/pressReleaseView.do?newsId=156066598)). In the analysis of 1992~2000, the high occurrence years (1994, 1995, 1998, 2000) overlapped with high temperatures and continuous rainfall in the heading stage (early to mid-August) for mid-late-growing species, 1993 had a lot of rain but low temperatures, and 1997 had high temperatures but little rain. There was little occurrence. heading stage When treated in a wet room for more than 24 hours after inoculation, the disease occurred at 10² CFU/mL ([Plant Disease Research 7(3):150-154, 2001](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200111921139724.page?lang=ko), Abstract). Overseas: Growth temperature is 11~40℃, optimal temperature is 30~35℃, especially large outbreaks occur at **high temperatures at night** ([Ham et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640401/), Epidemiology); In the United States, high summer night temperatures, long dews, high nitrogen, and excessive sowing promote it ([FSA7580](https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/pdf/FSA-7580.pdf), Favorable Conditions).",

      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Leaves develop stripes, and panicles may be malformed, sterile, or fail to emerge fully. Seedlings through early tillering are most susceptible; infection after maximum tillering produces milder symptoms (Lucid/IRRI). Incubation is 7–15 days after inoculation at the 3–7-leaf stage and 15–30 days after inoculation at the 9–15-leaf stage (Jeong 1974). [Source 1](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus) [Source 2](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub)",
        "source_urls": [

          "https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub"

        "contains_unverified": false

      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Leaves develop yellowish-white stripes, mottling, and necrotic streaks. Infected seedlings have folded, twisted, wilted, drooping leaves; plants are stunted, with fewer tillers and panicles, and white to brown malformed panicles (Lucid). Wang et al. 2022 instead describe slight stunting with normal tiller numbers. The drooping seedlings that dry out and die gave rise to the Japanese name Yurei Byo (ghost disease), according to the source cited in the original research. [Source 1](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus)",
        "source_urls": [

          "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/",

        "contains_unverified": false

      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "Domestic researchers state that **\"RSV symptoms are very difficult to distinguish from physiological disorders with the naked eye\"** ([Lee et al. 2004, Plant Disease Research 10(1):30–33](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200411922293908.page), abstract). Zinc deficiency shows dusty brown spots on the upper leaves and mid-green yellowing at the base of young leaves 2 to 4 weeks after transplanting ([Lucid Factsheet \"Zinc deficiency\"](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Zinc_deficiency.htm); This page does not directly compare RSV). Black-striped rice dwarf (RBSDV, also vectored by the small brown planthopper) has increased tillering, dark green leaves, and white to black waxy nodules on the leaf veins on the underside of the leaves. Grassy stunt (RGSV) has greatly increased tillering and leaves are short, straight, and light green to light yellow. Rice dwarf (RDV) has dark green leaves with fine yellow-white spots and increased tillering, and its insect vector is the green rice leafhopper ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/), Table 2·3).",

        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Yellow-white stripes and necrotic streaks on new leaves, drooping or twisted seedlings (ghost-like appearance), normal or reduced tillering, non-emergence of ears, or deformities ([Lucid Factsheet \"Stripe\"](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus).htm); [Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/)). There is a domestic statement that it is difficult to distinguish from physiological disorders, so photos are used only for the first screening.\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Close-up photos of the entire plant and new leaves, photos of rows near the rice paddy bank (more on the side of the rice paddy bank, decreasing towards the center) ([Jeong Bong-jo 1974](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub)), presence or absence of small brown planthopper, early transplantation/direct sowing, early-growing susceptible varieties (Woonkwang rice, Odae rice, Ilpoom rice, etc.) ([Lee et al. 2012](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf)), Insecticide treatment of the seedbed and whether it is adjacent to a barley field ([Seung-oh Yoo 2008](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf)), Whether it is on the west coast and when it flies.\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* RT-PCR detected approximately 1,023-bp RdRp and 969-bp CP products from diseased plants and small brown planthoppers (Lee et al. 2004, abstract). An ELISA assay for virus-carrying small brown planthoppers was mentioned in a Gyeonggi agricultural research report, available only as a search snippet. Sap inoculation is unsuitable because the virus is poorly transmitted through sap, according to the cited account.       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "The cited Korean study gives an optimum transmission temperature of 25–30 °C, rare or absent transmission at 15 °C or below, and five annual generations of the small brown planthopper in Korea. About 90% of offspring of two virus-carrying parents carry the virus through transovarial transmission; acquisition by nonviruliferous insects is about 7–9%, with third- to fifth-instar nymphs most efficient. Of 35 crop, pasture, and weed species tested, 21 were susceptible (Jeong 1974). A laboratory colony had a 52–63% virus-carrier rate, which is not a field estimate (Yi et al. 2015). The vector latent/circulation period is 5–21 days (Wang et al. 2022). Proposed contributors to the 2007 epidemic were untreated seedbeds, early-transplanted and direct-seeded rice providing food for overwintered viruliferous insects, warmer winters (Seocheon +0.8 °C; Buan +2.0 °C), and increased susceptible varieties (Yoo 2008). The first west-coast migration in 2012 was on May 28, concentrated in Jeonbuk and Chungnam, with counts of 1–302 insects (Lee et al. 2012). Risk is greatest when viruliferous planthoppers move from cereal crops to rice. [Source 1](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO197425720625117.pub) [Source 2](https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO201510659891088.do) [Source 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 4](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf) [Source 5](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf) [Source 6](https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/key-server/data/0e090d01-0209-460e-810c-0d060708030c/media/Html/Stripe_(Rice_stripe_virus)",

        "text": "Korea: National average incidence rate was about 6.5% in 1965, decreased by resistant cultivars (Nakdong rice) and pest control in the 1980s, **about 4,663 ha in Ganghwa in 2001, 14,137 ha nationwide in 2007, 21,541 ha on the west coast in 2009**, 525 ha in 2010, 7,397 ha in 2011; In the 2012 national survey, the incidence rate decreased from 19.9% in 2008 to 4.9% ([Lee et al. 2012](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO201205759624605.pdf), Text·Table 2·Fig. 3). In 2007, Seocheon occurred in 2,610 ha, or 25% of the total area ([Yoo Seung-oh 2008](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200856450901109.pdf)). Wikipedia's \"84% damage to Korean rice fields in 2007–08\" conflicts with domestic primary data (2008 outbreak area rate 19.9%), so domestic data is used) takes precedence ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_stripe_virus), Distribution). The area of occurrence by year since 2013 is unverified. Overseas: EPPO (updated 2020-06-23) lists China (restricted), Japan, North Korea, **South Korea \"Present, no details\"**, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the Russian Far East and South ([EPPO RSV000 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/RSV000/distribution)).       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "The principal vector is *Nephotettix cincticeps*; *N. nigropictus* and *Recilia dorsalis* also transmit the virus. Transmission is propagative, including transovarial transmission involving the symbiont *Candidatus* Sulcia muelleri (ICTV). The vector latent/circulation period is 12–25 days (Wang et al. 2022). Korean studies report five annual vector peaks and three disease peaks, with overwintered adults and second- and third-generation nymphs as major sources. At the distribution boundary in Uljin, viruliferous nymphs could not overwinter in the field. Feeding initially virus-free nymphs on infected ratoon rice for 11–30 days produced 13.0–18.2% overwintering virus carriers. Ratoon clump infection in a regularly affected Miryang area was 22.4–26.8% (Lee 1986). Temperature and humidity thresholds for transmission and disease were not verified. [Source 1](https://ictv.global/report/chapter/sedoreoviridae/sedoreoviridae/phytoreovirus) [Source 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9609659/) [Source 3](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO198630710156433.page)",

        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },

        "text": "The Korean disease name was not confirmed anywhere in the List of Plant Diseases in Korea·NCPMS·EPPO (unverified; no Korean search results) ([EPPO BALAOS](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS), Overview). However, **In Paragraph 1 of Annex 1 of the Enforcement Rules of the Plant Quarantine Act, the prohibited quarantine pest name is written as \"udbatta disease [*Balansia oryzae-sativae*]\"** ([KR-Rules Annex 1](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?gubun=&flSeq=163692257&bylClsCd=110201)).) Therefore, the name in the law is confirmed, and the name in the disease name list is unverified. The EPPO preferred name is *Balansia oryzae-sativae* Hashioka (BALAOS), the synonym is *Balansia oryzae*, *Ephelis oryzae* Sydow, and the English name is black choke of rice, false ergot, incense rod, udbatta disease ([EPPO BALAOS](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BALAOS)). There is a classification dispute. The ITS phylogenetic analysis of 33 *Ephelis* isolates from Japan, Korea, China, Nepal, and India pointed out that there was no basis for dividing *E. oryzae* and *E. japonica* and suggested ***E. japonica*** according to naming priority, and that *Balansia oryzae* was not validly published ([Tanaka et al. 2001](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2), Abstract). Japanese literature also equates *E. oryzae* (= *B. oryzae-sativae*) and adopts *E. japonica* ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008, JARQ 42(3)](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), Discussion).",

        "text": "Affects panicles at heading and flag leaves, where white fungal streaks develop along veins before heading.         "source_urls": [

      "f5_differentiation": {

        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* At heading, the entire panicle forms a single rod-like structure with a white to gray-black stromatal coating. [Source 1](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html) [Source 2](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf) [Source 3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2)\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Whether nearby grasses and weeds (alternative hosts such as *Isachne elegans*, *Cynodon dactylon*, *Pennisetum* sp., *Eragrostis tenuifolia*) have the same symptoms, and seed source ([TNAU](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/expert_system/paddy/cpdisudbtta.html), Mode of spread).\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Genus determination by *Ephelis* type conidium microscopic examination ([Tsukiboshi et al. 2008](https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/jarq/42-03-06_0.pdf), Discussion), ITS sequence analysis ([Tanaka et al. 2001](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mycological-research/article/phylogenetic-studies-of-ephelis-species-from-various-locations-and-hosts-in-asia/620F727E95233FBD11FC91864980E3C2)). prohibited quarantine pest, therefore, suspected cases must undergo morphological and molecular identification and confirmation by quarantine agencies in parallel.",

EPPO carries *Ditylenchus angustus* (Butler) Filipjev(DITYAN), synonym *Anguillulina angusta*, *Tylenchus angustus*, common names akhet-pet, dak pora, rice stem nematode, ufra disease ([EPPO DITYAN datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DITYAN/datasheet)). local names are ufra (India), dak pora (Bangladesh), akhet-pet (Myanmar), yadngo (Thailand), and tiem dot san (Vietnam). After Butler (1913) described it in East Bengal, Goodey (1932) and Filipjev (1936) transferred it to the genus ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Common Names·Pest Description).       "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "The nematode is an ectoparasite of above-ground tissues, especially young leaves, inflorescences, and young seed, and can be recovered from dried stems. It is absent from internodes below the growing point. Leaf yellowing occurs from seedling to flag-leaf stages; panicle symptoms appear after heading. First symptoms are observed about 2 months after transplanting, and early heading is the best survey stage (USDA CAPS 2016). [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf)",

        ],

      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "During the vegetative growth stage, yellowing and deformity of leaves, **white splash-shaped spots at the base of young leaves**, necrotic brown stains on leaves and leaf sheaths, blackening of upper internodes, twisting of bases of young leaves, swelling of lower nodes and irregular branches appear. After heading, the ears are wrinkled and empty, the ears and branches are twisted, **the ears are trapped in the swollen leaf sheath**, or only a part of them comes out. Dark brown patches appear on the field, and during harvest, healthy plants fall over, but infected plants (empty ears) stand upright ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Symptoms Fig. 2–6; [CDFA 2026](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf), Symptoms).",
        "source_urls": [

          "https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "The rice leaf nematode (*Aphelenchoides besseyi*, white tip) found in Korea is difficult to distinguish at low magnification because the damage and larval and female forms are similar. *A. besseyi* has an esophageal gland that largely overlaps the front of the intestine and has 3-4 projections at the end of the tail. Males do not have a bursa and have 2-4 rows of oocytes, while *D. angustus* males have a bursa and usually have 1 row of oocytes ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Easily Confused Pests·Pest Description). The primary source for comparison with stem borer pests (whiteheads) is unverified. It has been reported that zinc deficiency in soil and plants is related to ufra susceptibility (Miah et al. 1984), and there is a technology that brown spots on the damaged area may be the site of secondary invasion by *Fusarium*, *Sarocladium oryzae*, etc. ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Biology·Known Vectors).",
        "source_urls": [

        "contains_unverified": true

      "f5_differentiation": {
        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* White splash spots at the base of young leaves, twisted leaf bases and flag leaves, ears trapped in swollen leaf sheaths, black browning between upper internodes, dark brown patches in the field, and empty ears standing upright at harvest time ([USDA CAPS 2016](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf), Symptoms). Low-density infections are difficult to detect with the naked eye (same document, Survey). The judgment that the absence of borers or larvae in the stem cross section is a clue to distinguishing from pest damage is an inference.\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Deep or long-term flooding, irrigation water inflow route, history of imported seeds or plants, presence of stumps or ratoon rice.\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Extract nematodes by cutting dried leaves and stems into approximately 55-mm pieces, splitting them lengthwise, and soaking them for 24 hours; dissect young inflorescences under water, use a Baermann funnel for 24 hours, or use a mist chamber. Collect tissue above the panicle neck (USDA CAPS 2016). Identification uses tail shape and size, relative lengths of the stylet and post-uterine sac, and four lateral lines; females measure 0.8–1.2 mm, with a 10–11 µm stylet and V=78–80. Esterase/protein profiles and rDNA PCR help distinguish *Aphelenchoides*. As a prohibited quarantine pest in the original research, suspected findings require notification to the quarantine authority. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf)",

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "Infection is optimal at 27–30 °C, with a 10–20-day life cycle. Movement on leaves requires RH of at least 75%. Irrigation spreads nematodes; most die within days in water, but they can invade young rice within an hour. This is a major pest of deepwater rice flooded more than 50 cm for over a month, and occurs sporadically in irrigated and rainfed rice. At harvest, nematodes survive by anhydrobiosis inside dry glumes of lower spikelets, primarily as J4 juveniles. At least three generations occur per crop (USDA CAPS). Seed transmission remains disputed: Prasad & Varaprasad 2002 reported it, while Bridge & Starr 2007 and CABI 2021 assessed the risk as small (CDFA). Hosts include *Oryza* spp., *Leersia hexandra*, *Echinochloa colona*, *Sacciolepis interrupta*, and wheat. Reported yield losses are 20–90% in India/Thailand, 50–100% in Vietnam, and 40–60% in Bangladesh. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Ditylenchus-angustus-datasheet-2016.pdf) [Source 2](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ditylenchus-angustus.pdf)",

        ],

The Korean disease label is also used for rice brown spot caused by *B. oryzae*, so the crop must be specified; the two diseases must not be given the same English name. EPPO's preferred name is *Bipolaris maydis* (Nisikado & Miyake) Shoemaker (COCHHE); synonyms are *Cochliobolus heterostrophus*, *Drechslera maydis*, *Helminthosporium maydis*, and *Ophiobolus heterostrophus*. Infected seedlings may wilt and die 3 to 4 weeks after sowing, and early leaf infection can easily lead to stem rot ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202), Symptom Description). In Korea, it mainly occurs in the high temperature and humidity inland from **June to August**, and also occurs in early sowing tunnel cultivation in Jeju ([RDA press release 2025-06-16](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185), southern corn leaf blight paragraph).     "section_title": "Gray leaf spot — *Cercospora zeae-maydis*, *C. zeina*",
    "fields": {
      "f1_names": {
        "label": "Official names, scientific names, and synonyms",
        "text": "**Official Korean name: unverified.** No Korean name, including “gray leaf spot,” has been confirmed by authoritative sources. In the RDA 2025 press release, the description of \"spotted disease\" (gray to yellowish brown rectangular symptom, rare in the past, infection caused by soil spores splashed with rainwater) is similar to GLS, but the response cannot be confirmed due to the lack of a scientific name ([RDA press release 2025-06-16](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185), spotted disease paragraph). EPPO is *Cercospora zeae-maydis* Tehon & E.Y. Daniels (CERCZM), carrying the English name gray leaf spot of maize ([EPPO CERCZM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CERCZM)). ***C. zeina*** Crous & U. Braun (MB500863) is the existing 'Group II', and *C. zeae-maydis* is 'Group I', and it was confirmed that they are a separate species based on the ITS, EF-1α, histone H3, actin, and calmodulin sequences ([Crous et al. 2006, Studies in Mycology 55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/), Abstract·Taxonomy). GLS is a complex disease of two closely related species, and *C. zeina* is dominant in some subtropical regions of South Africa and China ([Li et al. 2026, J. Fungi 12(9):650](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/), Introduction).",

      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "It first appears in the lower leaves 2-3 weeks before heading ([CPN Encyclopedia GLS](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gray-leaf-spot-of-corn)). Yield loss mainly occurs when the 8-9 leaves above the spike (supplying more than 75% of the spike's carbohydrates) are infected, stem infection causes lodging, and chlorosis appears about 9 days after infection ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Symptoms·Yield loss).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gray-leaf-spot-of-corn",
          "https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Initially, brown and tan spots (0.2 in wide, 0.4 to 0.8 in long) fill the space between leaf veins, and yellow borders are **visible in backlight**. Mature lesions are limited to the leaf veins and are rectangular, blunt-tipped, tan to gray, up to 0.2 in wide and up to 2.8 in long. Gray spores appear, which is where the disease name comes from ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Symptoms). *C. zeina* lesions are bilateral, 2-3 mm wide, 5-40 mm long, light gray to light brown ([Crous et al. 2006](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/), *C. zeina* description).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view",
          "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "Early GLS is most confused with anthracnose (*Colletotrichum graminicola*), eyespot (*Kabatiella zeae*), and early common rust pustules (*Puccinia sorghi*). Common rust pustules can be seen when enlarged, and spores come out when bursting. Mature lesions are distinct, but early lesions “can be easily confused” ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Similar diseases). For the difference from SCLB, see Section 14 ④. Data for identifying abiotic disorders such as potassium deficiency and phytotoxicity are unsecured.",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f5_differentiation": {
        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Parallel rectangles limited to leaf veins, blunt tips, yellow border when backlit (early), progression from lower to upper leaves, gray spore layer. **It is impossible to distinguish between the two species through photographs.**\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Backlit photos, photos of leaves above and below the ears, continuous cropping, no-till, and surface residue coverage.\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* *C. zeae-maydis* grows faster in culture, produces cercosporin, and has longer conidiophores (up to 180 µm). *C. zeina* grows more slowly, has shorter conidiophores (up to 100 µm), and lacks the red pigment associated with cercosporin. Conidial sizes overlap. A histone-H3-based species-specific PCR assay has been developed (Crous et al. 2006). The original Korean regulatory research listed *C. zeae-maydis* only, making species identification important for quarantine decisions. [Source 1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/)",

          "f5b_extra_requests": "Backlit photos, photos of leaves above and below the ears, continuous cropping, no-till, and surface residue coverage.",
          "f5c_lab_tests": "*C. zeae-maydis* grows faster in culture, produces cercosporin, and has longer conidiophores (up to 180 µm). *C. zeina* grows more slowly, has shorter conidiophores (up to 100 µm), and lacks the red pigment associated with cercosporin. Conidial sizes overlap. A histone-H3-based species-specific PCR assay has been developed (Crous et al. 2006). The original Korean regulatory research listed *C. zeae-maydis* only, making species identification important for quarantine decisions. [Source 1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/)"
        }

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "**70~90 °F** (The original text was written together as \"25~32 °C\", but 70 °F is about 21 °C, so there is a possibility of conversion error, so it should be read as about 21~32 °C based on the original value of °F), with dew, rain, and irrigation **Free water for at least 12 hours, RH 90% or more**; Susceptible cultivars have an infection cycle of 14 to 21 days, conidium invades in 4 to 7 days, and up to 5,000 spores per 1 mm² lesion ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Disease cycle). It rarely survives in buried remains, and if more than 30% of the previous year's infected field surface remains, the likelihood of damage is high, and even 10% can cause significant losses. In Iowa, when reduced-tillage area increased from 55.1% to 77.9% from 1983 to 1997, the severity increased from 10% to 95% (same source, Residue/tillage). Reduced tillage, susceptible varieties, dense planting, and climate warming promote GLS ([Li et al. 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/), Introduction).",

          "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/"

      },

        "text": "Small yellow spots develop into powdery **brick-colored pustules (about 1/8 in, about 3 mm)** that are scattered or gathered together, and appear black when aged ([CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-rust-of-corn)).       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "High humidity, daytime temperatures 60 to 77 °F (about 16 to 25 °C), **night temperatures 65 to 70 °F (about 18 to 21 °C)**, **leaves wet at least 3 hours**; It does not winter in New York, but is brought in by the wind from the south every year, and completes its life cycle in *Oxalis* in tropical and subtropical regions. It is not transmitted through residues and is therefore unrelated to tillage ([Cornell Common Rust](https://www.vegetables.cornell.edu/pest-management/disease-factsheets/common-rust-of-sweet-corn), Disease cycle). CPN also notes that cool nights and high humidity are more severe in seed-production corn ([CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-rust-of-corn)).) and are associated with 18-49% yield loss under glass conditions ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Introduction).",

        "text": "Pustules usually appear first in the middle and upper canopy after VT; vegetative-stage occurrence is uncommon except in late-planted corn. Korean specimens were collected mainly in September–October, with pustules on both leaf surfaces and rarely on stems (Lee et al. 2025).         "text": "**Orange to tan pustules, approximately 1/16 in (1.5 mm) in diameter**, mostly on the front of the leaf, with only chlorosis visible on the back.       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "**Infection occurs after about 6 hours of leaf wetting**, and dew is often sufficient. **About 80 °F (27 °C)** and high humidity are advantageous. The incubation period is as short as 9 days, and one pustule produces spores for up to 8 days. Because it requires a living host and cannot survive on remnants, it does not winter in the north and is brought in by wind from the tropics every year. Alert methods such as residue management have no effect ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Disease cycle). The germination rate of urediniospores of domestic isolates was the highest (49%) at 25 ℃, similar at 20-30 ℃, rapidly decreased when the temperature exceeded 32 ℃, less than 2% at 38·40 ℃, and over 40% germinated within 9 hours at 25-28 ℃ ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.4 Fig. 6). Fungicide effectiveness is expected when the initial discovery stage is VT~R3, R5 is low, and R6 is absent ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Table 2).",

        "label": "Occurrence records in Korea and other countries",
        "text": "Korea: **New domestic record in 2025.** \"*P. polysora* is newly reported in Korea and was the prevalent species over *P. sorghi* among the collected samples\"([Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647, PMID 40792185](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Abstract). The collection distribution is 2 in Gangwon, 2 in Chungbuk, 3 in Chungnam, 23 in Jeonbuk, and 3 in Jeonnam. Collection was conducted between September and October 2021 and 2024 (e.g., Jeonju 2021-09-27, Yeongdong 2021-10-16, Hongcheon 2024-09-06, Buan 2024-10-05). There is the National Institute of Agricultural Sciences and the Agriculture, Forestry and Livestock Quarantine Headquarters (same source, 3.3·Table 1). The paper calls this the “first conclusive evidence” of domestic existence (Discussion). As a prior report, a team from Kyungpook National University reported southern rust infection in Jeju and Gunwi field trials in 2008 and 2009 at an academic conference (2013), but the reliability was evaluated to be limited due to the lack of microscopic and molecular evidence ([Nabais et al. 2013](https://repository.pertanian.go.id/items/10443e19-845b-46c3-8556-acde9ae9c092/full), snippet). Domestic quantity damage and occurrence area statistics are unverified. Overseas: It has recently become prevalent in China, and distribution and spread have also been reported in Japan (Lee et al. (quoted from the 2025 Introduction). There is a review that says it was first recorded in West Africa in 1949 and in China since 1972 (search snippet)([PMC11766486](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11766486/)).) Overseas distribution is not the basis for domestic occurrence.",

      "f1_names": {

        "text": "The official name in Korea is **common smut** (黑穗病, Smut), and Nongsaro writes the pathogen as ***Ustilago zeae*** (old synonym) ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), title·pathogen). 『Korean Plant Disease List』 (2004) also lists “common smut (Smut) by *Ustilago zeae*” (second citation) ([Han et al. 2015, Res.       "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "It occurs on male and female ears, stems, and leaves, and rarely on roots ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), Symptom Description). All actively growing or embryonic tissue is susceptible, and any above-ground area is affected **from seedling to maturity** ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Common Smut·Symptoms; [CPN Common Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-smut-of-corn)).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177",
          "http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html",

        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "The diseased area abnormally enlarges and becomes a **gall**. The large lump is more than 10 cm in diameter. It is initially covered in a glossy white membrane, but when it bursts, black powder (teliospore) comes out ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), symptom description). Or, it is surrounded by a greenish-white to silvery-white membrane and reaches a diameter of 15 cm when mature, and small hard nodules the size of peas appear on the leaves ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Fig. 1·2). None of the major ear rots produces a lump ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Corn smut).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177",
          "http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html",
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "Head smut is a seedling systemic infection where the spores are not wrapped in fleshy nodules, so it is only visible during the flowering period ([UNL CropWatch Head Smut](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut)), It is distinguished from common smut by the presence of **tangled filamentous vascular remnants** mixed with telia) ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Head Smut–Symptoms). It is distinguished from ear rots by the presence or absence of galls ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)).) Plants with galls on lower stems appear red in the fall and may be similar to aphid damage ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Common Smut paragraph 3).",
        "source_urls": [

        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Fleshy nodule wrapped in a silver-white membrane, black powder after membrane rupture, site of occurrence (stem, leaf, ear, tassel), size 10-15 cm. Ask about wounds from detasseling, hail, wind-blown soil, insects, or machinery; nitrogen and manure inputs; and rainfall and temperature during early growth (Illinois RPD 203).       "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "It occurs on male and fetassels, and rarely on leaves ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html); [PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)). **Infection occurs in the soil during the seedling stage, and symptoms become evident only at the flowering stage**([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut)), mycelium enters the undifferentiated spike and tassel tissue from the seedling meristem) sori ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Disease Cycle).",
        "source_urls": [

      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Sori consist of dark-brown to black teliospore masses initially covered by a thin grayish-white membrane that soon ruptures. Tangled thread-like vascular remnants remain among the spores; infected tassels usually lack pollen. Phyllody and teliospore streaks on leaves also occur (Illinois RPD 203). Wire-like tassel projections, finger-like ear proliferation, teardrop-shaped ears without silks, and dwarfing in some varieties are reported (UNL; PNW). [Source 1](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html) [Source 2](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut) [Source 3](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)",
        "source_urls": [
          "http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html",
          "https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut",
          "https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "It is easy to confuse with common smut, and is distinguished by the absence of fleshy lumps and the presence of vascular threads ([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut); [Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html)).) The possibility of foliar symptoms being confused with other causes such as downy mildews is unverified as there is no source for comparison.",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut",

        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Tassels and ears are replaced by spore masses. [Source 1](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548) [Source 2](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html) [Source 3](https://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=1265069)\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Whether multiple years in the same field (soil teliospore survival 5 to 7 years ([PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)) or more than 3 years ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html))), Infection of all ears on one plant (systemic infection) ([Bugwood 1265069 caption](https://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=1265069)), Seed source.\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Teliospores are reddish-brown to black, spherical to subspherical, prominently spiny, and 9–14 µm across; sporidia are colorless and 7–15 µm long (Illinois RPD 203).       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "It is infected even at a soil temperature of **15 ℃, and is more likely to be infected at 20-30 ℃ ([PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548), Cause and disease cycle). **Low soil moisture (15-25% w/w)** is optimal for seedling infection, and temperature is more important than soil moisture for infection (part of original sentence damaged). High soil moisture and winter soil temperatures above 0 ℃ lower the survival rate of teliospore, which is abundant in clay loam soils and worsens with nitrogen deficiency ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Last paragraph of Disease Cycle; [CPN Head Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/head-smut-of-corn)). Early sowing can avoid germination temperatures), and seeds are not the main source of infection, but diseases can be introduced through surface spores.       "f1_names": {
        "label": "Official names, scientific names, and synonyms",
        "text": "Nongsaro corn **ear rot**(穗腐病, Ear rot) writes the pathogen as ***Gibberella fujikuroi*** and specifies corn in the text ([Nongsaro D00001173](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173), title·pathogen·environment of occurrence). 『Korean Plant Disease List』 (2004) lists \"ear rot caused by *G. fujikuroi*\" and \"stalk rot caused by *F. moniliforme*\" (second citation), and it is said that the *G. fujikuroi* species complex, previously called *F. moniliforme*, was divided into several species. Explain ([Han et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280), p.281). The most common overseas causal pathogen are *F. verticillioides*, *F. proliferatum*, and *F. subglutinans*, and the former two species are related to fumonisin ([UT Crops Fusarium Ear Rot](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/), Causal Species; [CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)). **Caution:** In EPPO Since *G. fujikuroi* is a synonym for the rice bakanae disease bacteria *F. fujikuroi* ([EPPO GIBBFU](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/GIBBFU)) Nongsaro), it is confusing if the scientific name is translated as is. In addition, Annex 3 of the notice adds *Gibberella zeae* to corn “ear rot” (Section 21). The EPPO code of *F. verticillioides* was identified as FUSAVR in the quarantine note. The judgment that Nongsaro ear rot corresponds to overseas Fusarium ear rot is an inference based on symptoms and conditions, and the scientific name reflected in the latest edition of NCPMS/Plant Disease List is unverified.",

      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Infection occurs through silks, insect injuries, and kernel wounds. *F. verticillioides* can also grow systemically through the stalk into the ear (CPN). Disease can continue beyond R6 until kernel moisture falls below 18% (UT Crops). Scouting should begin in late dent (R5). Disease also occurs in storage (Nongsaro). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/fusarium-ear-rot-of-corn) [Source 2](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/) [Source 3](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots) [Source 4](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173)",
        "source_urls": [

          "https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "The shell and kernels are partially pink to reddish brown, pink fluffy mold is abundant around bug holes and wounds, and white stripes appear on late-stage infected kernels ([Nongsaro D00001173](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173), symptom description). The grains are discolored **scattered or in groups**, and white, pink, and purple mold is visible, and white stripes caused by fungal growth under the skin are called **'starbursts'**. It often occurs on grains damaged by the European light moth, the common tobacco moth, and birds ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Fig. 5·6; [UT Crops](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/)).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173",
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots",
          "https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "CPN Ear Rots criteria: Gibberella has pink to red mold and bract and silk adhesion (mummification) starting from the tip of the ear, Aspergillus has olive green powder (aflatoxin) at the tip of the ear, Diplodia has dense white to gray mold and black pycnidia that progresses from the base to the tip, Penicillium has blue-green powder and 'blue-eye' grains (some ochratoxin), and Trichoderma is dark blue-green. Spores and early germination, Cladosporium has black-green grains and black stripes, Nigrospora has black spores that fall off when rubbed ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), each item). The source for differentiation from insect/bird damage itself and physiological grain splitting is unverified. Nongsaro also writes that it is common in fruits with wounds from birds and insects.",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f5_differentiation": {
        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Scattered/clustered distribution at grain level, white to pink/purple downy mildew, starburst white stripes, overlap with insect/bird damage areas, start of ear tip (Gibberella differentiation), base start and black pycnidia (Diplodia differentiation), olive green/blue-green shade (Aspergillus/Penicillium differentiation). **Distinguishing the causative species (*F. verticillioides*/*F. proliferatum*/*F. subglutinans*) and determining fumonisin are impossible with photographs.**\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* High temperature/drying before and after seeding, ear damaging pests, hail, Bt traits, harvest delay, storage moisture ([UT Crops](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/); [CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)).\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Laboratory tests are often the only reliable method for identifying ear rot·mycotoxins, and **fumonisin levels can be high even when the disease appears superficial** ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Diagnosis·Mycotoxin). It is recommended that moldy corn be tested for toxins before feeding ([CPN Fusarium Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/fusarium-ear-rot-of-corn)).) Morphology and EF1α sequence analysis were used to identify domestic FFSC species (case of stump rot) ([Han et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280), p.281). For comparison of toxin measurement methods, see Section 21, ⑤.",

The same pathogen also causes stalk rot in corn and Fusarium head blight in wheat (CPN).       "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "At harvest time, infection usually begins at the tip of the ear and causes discoloration and rot inside**. During storage, it rots anywhere, and many pink to red mycelium and spore masses are formed between the bracts and the ear. If these ears are used as feed for pigs, etc., they cause poisoning ([Nongsaro Attachment 29198](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198), 1. symptoms). If there is a lot of mold, the silks and bracts stick to the ear and become **'mummified'**. It is easy to recognize in an intact ear, but it is difficult to identify after shelling ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Gibberella Fig. 8; [CPN Gibberella Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gibberella-ear-rot-of-corn)).",

      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Corn, especially sweet corn, is the main host; the cited host list also includes *Dracaena sanderiana*, *Oryza sativa*, *Saccharum officinarum*, and *Setaria pumila*. Symptoms affect leaves (streaks), stalks (vascular tissue and pith cavities), tassels (early emergence and discoloration), and seed (deep invasion without reaching the embryo). Wilt is particularly important in sweet corn, while the leaf-blight phase occurs after tasseling in dent corn (EPPO). [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet)",

        "text": "In the wilt phase, susceptible plants wilt rapidly, pale-green to yellow streaks dry to brown, tassels emerge prematurely and become discolored, and cavities may form in the stalk pith. In the leaf-blight phase after tasseling, streaks begin at corn flea-beetle feeding wounds and entire leaves can become straw-colored (EPPO). Lesions generally follow the veins with wavy margins; pale-yellow bacterial ooze may emerge from cut stalks (CPN). [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet) [Source 2](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/stewarts-disease-of-corn)",

        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "Goss's wilt also produces seedling dieback and lesion, but **freckles** (dark green to black water-soaked spots within the lesion) are found only on Goss's wilt. Stewart's disease has been rarely recorded since the early 2000s, so it is recommended that suspected samples be sent to a diagnostic institution. NCLB is a 1-4 inch cigar-shaped lesion with even edges and no freckles or bacterial leakage ([CPN Goss's Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Look-alikes). For drought and nutrient deficiency, refer to the general criteria in the Goss disease document, which states that there are no freckles, gloss spills, or bacterial spills (same source). No data related to hail and wind injuries was found.",

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "The main insect vector in the United States is the corn flea beetle (*Chaetocnema pulicaria*), which overwinters as an adult and can retain bacteria throughout its life. **If the average daily temperature from December to February is above freezing, insect vectors can survive and a severe outbreak is possible, and if it is below -3℃, a severe outbreak is unlikely** (based on the U.S. surveillance model). If there is a lot of ammonium N and P, susceptibility increases, if there is a lot of Ca·K, it decreases, and high temperatures make the disease worse. Bacteria in seeds disappear after 200-250 days at 8-15 ℃ and 110-120 days at 20-25 ℃ (Guo et al. 1987) Seed → seedling transmission rate is “very low” ([EPPO ERWIST datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet), Biology·Phytosanitary measures). The Fahrenheit winter temperature index (sum of monthly average °F for December, January, and February) is <90 usually not occurred, 90 to 100 is moderate, and >100 is usually severe ([Mulrooney 2009, Univ. of Delaware](https://sites.udel.edu/weeklycropupdate/?p=771)). Domestic *C. pulicaria* distribution is unverified, so domestic risk cannot be determined.",
