  {
    "no": 23,
    "crop": "corn",
    "user_name": "Goss’s bacterial wilt and leaf blight",
    "official_kr_name": "Unverified",
    "scientific_name": "*Clavibacter nebraskensis*",
    "kr_occurrence": "Domestic outbreak records unverified",
    "kr_quarantine": "regulated quarantine pest (listed under the old scientific name)",
    "commercial_image": "Available (2 pieces of Bugwood)",
    "section_title": "Goss’s bacterial wilt and leaf blight — *Clavibacter nebraskensis*",
    "fields": {
      "f1_names": {
        "label": "Official names, scientific names, and synonyms",
        "text": "**Official Korean disease name: unverified.** Current scientific name is *Clavibacter nebraskensis* (Davis et al.) Li et al.(EPPO CORBNE), synonym is ***Clavibacter michiganensis* subsp. *nebraskensis***, *Corynebacterium michiganense* pv./subsp. *nebraskense*, *Corynebacterium nebraskense*, English name is Goss's wilt, leaf freckles of maize ([EPPO CORBNE](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CORBNE), Overview). Since the Korean examination lists the old academic name, it will be missed if you search only by the current name.",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CORBNE"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "Infection can occur at any growth stage. Infection before V6 is more likely to become systemic and cause wilt and death, with systemic wilt usually first seen at V2–V6. Later infection generally causes leaf blight. Symptoms are most conspicuous after silking (R1). Leaves, vascular tissue, and stalk pith are affected (CPN). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight)",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "The common leaf-blight phase begins as pale-green water-soaked streaks, becoming tan to gray-brown lesions with wavy edges parallel to the veins. Dark-green to black water-soaked freckles within lesions, translucent when backlit, are described as diagnostic of Goss’s wilt. Small orange bacterial-ooze droplets form when wet, leaving a dried-varnish-like sheen after drying. Systemic wilt includes slimy stalk rot, wilting, and discoloration of xylem and stalk pith (CPN). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight)",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "CPN look-alikes criteria: NCLB (1 to 4 in cigar shape with even edges, no freckles or bacterial shedding; some hybrids do not produce freckles, making distinction increasingly difficult), Stewart's wilt (distinguished by presence or absence of freckles), bacterial streak disease (*Xanthomonas vasicola* pv. *vasculorum*; Narrower tan to yellow lesions, bright yellow in backlight, no freckles, bacterial shedding possible on both sides), Diplodia leaf streak (bright yellow halo, pycnidia), **nutrient deficiency (N, K, P) and drought/leaf tip die** (no freckles, glossy shedding, or bacterial shedding, drought causes uniform browning from the leaf margins inward) ([CPN Goss's) Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Look-alikes). Ilso is not mentioned (unverified).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f5_differentiation": {

        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Backlit photos of the lesion show translucency of freckles, glossy exudate on the lesion surface, lesion at the edges of the undulations, and discoloration of the vascular bundles on the longitudinal section of the stem.       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "It occurs easily around **27 ℃ (80 °F)** and can be suppressed** above 35 ℃ or below 21 ℃. **Hail, wind, sandstorms, storms** Wounds are entry points and irrigation can help progress but is not required. Survival is granted if you survive **at least 10-15 months** in surface remnants and are buried. Risk factors include susceptible hybrids, reduced tillage, and continuous cropping of fields with a history of occurrence, and alternative hosts include sorghum, Italian ryegrass, sudangrass, foxtails, Johnson grass, and crabgrass. The cited datasheet describes particularly high pathogenicity among corn downy-mildew pathogens, losses of 40–60% in corn, and an 8% nationwide loss in the Philippines in 1974–75.       "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "Conidia are formed at **18~23 ℃**, germinate at 10~35 ℃, and infection rate is highest above 16 ℃ (Bonde et al. 1992). For conidia formation, germination, and infection, **night temperature of 21~26℃**(Dalmacio & Raymundo 1972), high humidity, and **leaf surface water film in the dark for more than 4~5 hours**(Exconde 1970) are required. Conidia cannot germinate when exposed to sunlight, wind, and low humidity for 1 to 2 hours. The number of systemic infections is positively correlated with humidity, spore load, and rainfall, and negatively correlated with temperature and sunlight. If seed moisture is **less than 14%**, there is no seed transmission (Exconde 1976) ([USDA CAPS Corn datasheet](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.2 Biology and Ecology).",

        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "It is clearly bordered by a narrow chlorosis/yellow stripe with a width of **3~7 mm** and is divided into leaf veins, and in some genotypes, it turns red to purple.         "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "Sporangia form at 22–25 °C and release zoospores at 20–22 °C; zoospores germinate at 15–30 °C. Oospores are more abundant above 28 °C (Payak 1975). Soil temperatures of 28–32 °C favor disease. The cited account describes low incidence with annual rainfall of 4–60 cm, intermediate incidence at 60–100 cm, and high incidence at 100–200 cm. Zoospore infection requires 12 hours of leaf wetness. Primary inoculum consists of oospores in soil residue, surviving up to 4 years (Singh 1971a); secondary spread occurs through rain splash and contact, with a maximum trapping distance of 1.65 m. Seed transmission is below 1% (Lal & Prasad 1989); transmission does not occur after storage for more than 4 weeks at seed moisture below 14%. The pathogen can overwinter in crabgrass (USDA CAPS).     "official_kr_name": "Unverified",
    "scientific_name": "MCMV (*Machlomovirus zeae*) + a coinfecting virus in the family Potyviridae (e.g., SCMV)",
    "kr_occurrence": "Domestic outbreak records unverified",
    "kr_quarantine": "MCMV regulated quarantine pest; SCMV not listed(check)",
    "commercial_image": "None (MLN symptoms only NC-SA)",
    "section_title": "Maize lethal necrosis — MCMV (*Machlomovirus zeae*) + a coinfecting virus in the family Potyviridae (e.g., SCMV)",
    "fields": {
      "f1_names": {
        "label": "Official names, scientific names, and synonyms",
        "text": "An official Korean disease name was not verified; the Korean working labels in the original notes were informal. Maize lethal necrosis (MLN) results from synergistic coinfection with maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) and another cereal-infecting virus in the family Potyviridae, such as SCMV, MDMV, or WSMV. These are not all members of the genus *Potyvirus*: WSMV belongs to *Tritimovirus*. MCMV is associated with species *Machlomovirus zeae* (EPPO MCMV00; Tombusviridae), synonym Maize chlorotic mottle machlomovirus. EPPO gives *Potyvirus sacchari* for SCMV (SCMV00) and *Potyvirus zeananus* for MDMV (MDMV00). Johnsongrass mosaic virus isolates may also be associated with MLN in East Africa (Prasanna et al. 2020). [Source 1](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/MCMV00) [Source 3](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf) [Source 4](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCMV00/distribution) [Source 5](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/MDMV00) [Source 6](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943)",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/",
          "https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/MCMV00",
          "https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf",
          "https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCMV00/distribution",

        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f2_parts_stages": {
        "label": "Affected plant parts and growth stages",
        "text": "From the seedling stage to maturity, **all growth stages are susceptible** ([CIMMYT Causes & Symptoms](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)),) The earlier the infection, the greater the damage and the entire harvest may be lost if infected early in the growing season ([CIMMYT MLN portal](https://mln.cimmyt.org/); [CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1).",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/",
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/",
          "https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f3_symptoms": {
        "label": "Major symptoms",
        "text": "Early symptoms are mosaic and chlorotic mottling, followed by necrosis beginning at leaf margins, death of the growing point (dead heart), premature husk drying, and poorly filled or sterile ears. SCMV alone causes mild mosaic/mottling; MCMV alone can cause shortened internodes, severe chlorotic mottling, and leaf necrosis (CIMMYT flyer). Kenya's first report describes mottling spreading from the base of young whorl leaves toward their tips, necrosis progressing from margins to midribs, and dead heart (Wangai et al. 2012, Plant Disease 96:1582; search snippet only, full text HTTP 403). MCMV-only severity varies with genotype, infection stage, environment, isolate, and coinfecting viruses; MLN is generally more severe (CDFA). Reported losses in affected Kenyan counties in 2012–2013 were 23–100%; national losses in 2013 were approximately 500,000 tonnes (US$180 million) (Prasanna et al. 2020). [Source 1](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf) [Source 2](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/2012/October/Pages/96_10_1582.3.aspx) [Source 3](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf) [Source 4](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943)",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf",
          "https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/2012/October/Pages/96_10_1582.3.aspx",
          "https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf",
          "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": false
      },
      "f4_confusions": {
        "label": "Similar diseases and abiotic disorders",
        "text": "MCMV or SCMV alone are usually mild, but together they produce a rapid synergistic effect ([CIMMYT Causes & Symptoms](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)),) MCMV alone can also cause significant losses ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), Abstract). Therefore, it is not possible to definitively distinguish between MCMV alone and MLN using only photos (inference). The only reference to confusion with drought, trace element deficiency, and stem moth damage is low-quality secondary data (SlideShare, original text not available) ([SlideShare](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/mln-disease-and-its-management-2015/55609041)). Standard for differentiation from nitrogen deficiency (lower leaf V-shaped yellowing), MSV, and domestic report MYMV). Primary data was not found (unverified).",
        "source_urls": [

        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f5_differentiation": {
        "label": "Additional photographs, questions, and diagnostic tests",
        "text": "*Features assessable in photographs:* Chlorosis spots (proximal) at the base of young leaf blades, necrosis progressing from the leaf margin to the midrib, dead heart (stem longitudinal section), early drying of bracts, poor ear filling, distribution within the field (more at the margins in the Kenyan report). In the final necrosis stage, photographic judgment is impossible due to MCMV alone, drought, and nutrient stress.\n*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Density of thrips, leaf beetles, and aphids, seed source (imported or not), continuous cropping and absence of a fallow season, surrounding grasses and weeds ([CIMMYT Flyer](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf); [CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)). **ImmunoStrip** detects leaf juice antigens within 30 minutes and can be used by non-experts, so it is used for field surveys ([CIMMYT MLN Diagnostic Techniques](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-diagnostic-techniques/)).\n*Features requiring laboratory tests:* DAS-ELISA (leaf·insect vector·seed identification test), PCR/RT-PCR, LAMP (same source). RT-PCR is more sensitive than ELISA, NGS is only available in specialized diagnostic laboratories, and **SCMV is highly variable, so serological results may be inconsistent** ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), 4. MLN diagnostics). The report that seed RT-PCR/RT-qPCR is more than 3,000 times more sensitive than commercial ELISA is a search snippet ([Bernardo et al. 2023](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9901749/)). **Confirmation of MLN requires detection of MCMV and potyvirus respectively**([CIMMYT Diagnostic Techniques](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-diagnostic-techniques/)). MCMV is a regulated quarantine pest, so official confirmation is required.",

      "f6_conditions": {
        "label": "Conditions favoring disease and supporting evidence",
        "text": "MCMV is transmitted by thrips and leaf beetles, and potyvirus is transmitted by aphids. There is also mechanical transmission through infected/contaminated seeds, infected soil/remnants, and agricultural machinery ([CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)). MCMV insect vectors are leaf beetles such as corn rootworms in the central United States, and corn thrips *Frankliniella williamsi* in Hawaii ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1). Seed transmission rates vary between sources: approximately 0.03–0.04% in the early United States ([CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)), <0.04% (Jensen et al. 1991)·Kenya 0.059% ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), paragraph 66), **approximately 0.004%** (cultivation test over 85,000 grains, Bernardo et al. 2023; The virus is mainly found in the pericarp and pedicel, but not in the embryo and endosperm) ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1). CIMMYT recommends a two-month corn-free season, legume crop rotation, weed removal, and a ban on using infected field seeds, suggesting that continuous cropping and year-round cultivation are risk factors ([CIMMYT Flyer](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf)). **Temperature and humidity thresholds not found (unverified).**",
        "source_urls": [
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/",
          "https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf",
          "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943",
          "https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf"
        ],
        "contains_unverified": true
      },
      "f7_occurrence": {
        "label": "Occurrence records in Korea and other countries",
        "text": "Korea: **MCMV, SCMV, and MLN all have domestic occurrence records unverified.** There is no Korea in the MCMV distribution of CABI 2026 (CDFA cited) and Prasanna 2020, and there is no Korea in the EPPO SCMV Asia distribution (including Japan, Taiwan, and China) ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), Worldwide Distribution; [EPPO SCMV00 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCMV00/distribution)). absence) It has not been confirmed. For MDMV, there is a paper on genetic analysis of resistance by domestic researchers in 1985, but the abstract does not mention whether the inoculum was a domestic isolate or whether it occurred domestically ([Heo et al. 1985](https://www.koreascience.kr/article/JAKO198530710155411.page)). New reports of domestic corn viruses include Maize yellow mosaic virus, unrelated to MLN (check only the title) ([Plant Disease PDN](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-11-17-1767-PDN)). Overseas: MCMV first reported in Peru (1974), later in the United States (Kansas corn lethal necrosis), Argentina, Thailand, Mexico, China, Kenya (first detected in September 2011), Uganda, Rwanda, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Taiwan, Ecuador, Spain ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), Introduction). CIMMYT lists Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Burundi as confirmed countries, but the text is inconsistent as it says \"six eastern African nations\" ([CIMMYT MLN portal](https://mln.cimmyt.org/); [MLN Distribution](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-distribution-and-spread-in-africa/)).)
